picks.style: roman wedding prophecy, kithara and low frame drum, layered male and female voices, spinning-wheel pulse, incantatory, building to dread
picks.why: The Fates' song with its hammering refrain 'run, drawing the thread, run, spindles!' — a built-in chorus wrapped around the birth of Achilles.

picks.style: latin epithalamium, antiphonal choirs of youths and maidens, aulos and lyre, alternating, evening-lit, tender then keen
picks.why: The walled-garden flower — untouched, then plucked and wanted by no one — Catullus's most quoted image, inside an answering-song already built for two choirs.

picks.style: latin tragic lament, solo female voice, lyre and low bowed strings, rubato, bitter, keening
picks.why: Ariadne abandoned: 'let no woman give credence to man's oath' — a complete, furious aria that needs no context.

picks.style: greek pastoral idyll, syrinx and lyre over soft drone, warm tenor, unhurried, sunlit, drowsy
picks.why: The harvest-home grove — cicadas, bees, pears at the feet, 'all breathed of rich summer' — the most beautiful landscape in Greek pastoral.

picks.style: amoebean shepherd's song, twin panpipes and hand drum, two answering male voices, call-and-response, lilting, rustic
picks.why: 'Spring everywhere, everywhere the meadows' — an antiphonal duet with the refrain shape already in the text, each stanza turning on 'but if she goes away'.

picks.style: sicilian pastoral air, single reed pipe and plucked lyre, plain low voice, slow, sea-facing, contented
picks.why: 'May I not have the land of Pelops, nor talents of gold... but under this rock will I sing, holding you in my arms' — a whole ethic of love in one refusal.

picks.style: georgian devotional air, chamber organ and viola da gamba, frail warm soprano, slow, hymn-like, consoling
picks.why: 'Domestic Love! assuasive power! Life's ruby gem' — an invocation written from a sickbed, plain and steady where the epic verse is ornate.

picks.style: english pastoral lyric, harp and flute, clear female voice, flowing, gentle, riverine
picks.why: The Vartree at morning and noon — dew, silver tide, chesnut glooms; a clean landscape song with real light in it.

picks.style: irish ballad, uilleann pipes and bodhran, keening female voice, modal, mournful, strophic
picks.why: 'Remember still in fury's hour the murdered youths of Glenmalure' — a rebellion ballad that ends on a plea a listener can carry away whole.

picks.style: english nocturne, chamber organ and muted strings, hushed baritone, very slow, floating, becalmed
picks.why: A hymn to Sleep: midnight looking down on earth and main, birds hushed, only the brook still murmuring — the quietest thing in the book.

picks.style: georgian ode setting, harpsichord and oboe, light tenor, pastoral, lilting, chamber
picks.why: Horace in the garden with the wandering bee — a clean opening, concrete, and short-lined enough to sing.

picks.style: baroque dramatic aria, agitated strings and continuo, urgent alto, minor key, stalking, unsettled
picks.why: Suspicion arriving as a sorceress with her torch steeped in gall and her garments dripping — a real personification with menace.

picks.style: eighteenth-century hymn-ode, harpsichord and strings, clear soprano, stately, nocturnal, measured
picks.why: The Ode to Wisdom — 'the solitary bird of night... quits his time-shook tow'r' — Carter's best-known lyric, and it was set to music in her own century.

picks.style: english art song, fortepiano and cello, reflective mezzo, gently rocking, tidal, introspective
picks.why: 'Thou restless fluctuating deep... in thy for ever varying form my own inconstant self I find' — the whole conceit lands in four lines.

picks.style: georgian ode, viola da gamba and chamber organ, contralto, slow, shadowed, processional
picks.why: 'Come, Melancholy! silent power, companion of my lonely hour' — a clean invocation with the yew grove and the retreat from folly's noisy stream.

picks.style: roman georgic, shepherd's pipe and plucked lyre, warm baritone, unhurried, sunlit, rustic
picks.why: Driving the flock out at first light while the turf is still hoary, then into the shade of Jove's great oak — the one passage here that is pure landscape.

picks.style: latin bee-hymn, soft aulos and shaken rattle, murmuring male voices, humming drone, light, midsummer
picks.why: New kings leading out the infant swarms under a wild-olive, bees resting on bridges to dry their wings — concrete and strangely tender.

picks.style: chartist protest ballad, industrial folk, anvil percussion and fiddle, gritty male chorus, driving, marching
picks.why: The Steam King as a one-armed Moloch fed on children — a factory-age ballad already written in singable quatrains.

picks.style: workers' anthem, hammered percussion, massed unison voices, insurgent, accelerating, defiant
picks.why: 'Then down with the King, the Moloch King, ye working millions all' — the rallying half of the same song, built to be shouted back.

picks.style: german classical lied, fortepiano and light strings, wry baritone, epigrammatic, brisk, chamber
picks.why: Schiller's joke on Kantian duty — serve your friends only after learning to despise them — a complete two-voice epigram.
